strong.label: Strong Connection
strong.description: Direct prerequisite — the later topic assumes real fluency here.

related.label: Related Topic
related.description: Meaningful conceptual overlap, but not a hard prerequisite.

weak.label: Weak Interaction
weak.description: Helpful background, low urgency — a distant echo, not a dependency.

connections.note: Atomic view of matter underpins electron configurations and the quantum model.
Molarity/solution concentration is the direct foundation for solution chemistry.
Early exposure to chemical bonds feeds into formal Lewis theory.
Math fundamentals resurface in analytical statistics, but are assumed mastered by then.
Measurement/units habits carry into experimental error and statistics.
First exposure to quantum ideas is formalized in Quantum I.
Electron configuration rules get their rigorous QM derivation here.
Periodic trends are revisited and deepened in Inorganic I.
Lewis theory is the springboard for MO theory and symmetry-based bonding.
VSEPR shapes matter again for conformations/stereochemistry.
Intro nomenclature and functional groups are reviewed before Organic I builds on them.
Ideal gas law is extended to real-gas behaviour and van der Waals corrections.
Kinetic theory intuition echoes faintly in particle-in-a-box/QM systems.
Kinetics is retaught with mechanisms, steady-state approximation, and Arrhenius depth.
Equilibrium constant concepts extend directly into Le Chatelier/Van't Hoff.
Acid-base fundamentals are prerequisite for polyprotic/analytical acid-base equilibria.
Acid-base theory recurs through a structural/periodic lens in Inorganic I.
Acid/base strength reasoning reappears for organic mechanism arguments.
Titration/Ksp basics extend into precipitation titrations and gravimetric analysis.
Gibbs energy module is prerequisite groundwork for the formal First Law treatment.
Entropy/second-law concepts are rebuilt rigorously with the Carnot cycle and third law.
The analytical process and error analysis underlie every separation technique that follows.
Intro chromatography concepts are the direct basis for full GC theory.
Same separations foundation carries into HPLC/SFC.
Beer's law and atomic spectroscopy basics are extended into full instrumental treatment.
Spectrophotometry intuition helps but mass spec is a largely new instrumental family.
Potentiometry and electrode fundamentals are prerequisite for electroanalytical techniques.
Foundational descriptive chemistry is assumed, then extended.
Intro to coordination compounds is essential groundwork for a full course on them.
Molecular symmetry is directly reused for point groups in Inorganic II.
MO theory is the backbone of the advanced bonding unit.
General kinetics tools are applied to inorganic reaction mechanisms.
Structure/stereochemistry fundamentals are required to interpret structural elucidation data.
Alkene reactivity patterns inform carbonyl/aromatic reaction mechanisms.
Substitution/elimination products are the ones you'll confirm with spectroscopy.
Organic bonding concepts loosely echo symmetry/MO ideas but aren't emphasized there.
Operator/wavefunction formalism is background context, not required, for spectrophotometry.
